impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 applies differently to method claims reciting functional genus limitations, specifically whether broad method claims covering all humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for treating headache are adequately enabled.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method claims for treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies against an enablement challenge by Eli Lilly. Judge Dyk dissented, arguing the panel's holding undermines Amgen v. Sanofi enablement standards for method claims and sustains overly broad claims that will stifle medical innovation. The denial preserves the panel's approach distinguishing method claims from composition claims for enablement purposes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims benefit from a more permissive enablement standard, potentially preserving valuable pharmaceutical and biotech patent portfolios covering genus-level antibody treatments.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitor companies and generic/biosimilar manufacturers face broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, potentially increasing licensing costs and delaying market entry for competing biologics.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee such that the licensee could sue for infringement in its own name without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee had 'ceased business operations' triggering automatic termination of the agreement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that TexasLDPC's exclusive license from Texas A&M University conveyed all substantial rights in the asserted patents, granting it standing to sue without joining A&M. The court also held that TexasLDPC had not ceased business operations merely by shifting to patent enforcement activities. This clarifies when an exclusive license is tantamount to an assignment for standing purposes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from confirmation that enforcement-focused business models do not constitute cessation of operations, and that comprehensive exclusive licenses can confer standalone litigation rights.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on challenging licensee standing, and technology companies face continued exposure to suits by exclusive licensees without the patent owner's direct involvement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert and in overturning the jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously excluded damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of breach of contract damages, reinstating the jury's award. The decision provides significant guidance on proper damages methodologies in trade secret misappropriation cases involving complex software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and trade secret owners benefit from broader acceptance of damages models and reinstatement of jury awards, strengthening enforcement of trade secret rights in technology licensing relationships.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal alternatives to licensed software face increased liability exposure for trade secret misappropriation, with potentially larger damages awards surviving post-trial challenges.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results without specifying which method defines the claimed range.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of the '287 patent are invalid as indefinite because the MVTR limitation could be measured using different testing methods (upright vs. inverted cup methods) that produce materially different results, and the specification failed to specify which method should be used. The patent's reference to ASTM E96-94 did not cure the ambiguity because that standard itself permits significant variability in testing conditions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in the outdoor apparel and materials industries gain a strong defense where patent claims incorporate performance metrics measurable by multiple methods yielding different results.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders claiming functional performance ranges must ensure their specifications clearly identify a single testing methodology; failure to do so risks invalidation of potentially valuable material science and textile patents.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform signal constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents directed to non-uniform constellations, while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents. The court also affirmed the denial of LG's JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This decision provides important guidance on the boundary between patent-eligible and ineligible subject matter in digital communications technology standards.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims tied to specific technical implementations in communications standards may preserve eligibility, and the affirmance of infringement and damages findings supports enforcement of standard-essential patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Consumer electronics manufacturers implementing industry standards face continued patent infringement liability, and the partial vacatur on eligibility creates uncertainty about the patentability of constellation design innovations.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for indefiniteness or lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed final judgment of invalidity but on alternative grounds, reversing the district court's indefiniteness ruling while holding the claims invalid for lack of enablement. The court found that while the claims were not indefinite, they failed the enablement requirement because the specification did not enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention. This case illustrates the interplay between indefiniteness and enablement defenses.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative enablement grounds even when the district court's indefiniteness analysis was incorrect, providing multiple avenues to challenge overly broad patent claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face heightened scrutiny of enablement for claims with broad functional language, even when claims survive indefiniteness challenges.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Hatch-Waxman patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the asserted claims of Exelixis's malate salt patents have adequate written description, upholding the district court's finding that the specification sufficiently described crystalline cabozantinib (L)-malate. The decision reinforces the validity of pharmaceutical polymorph patents protecting the cancer drug Cabometyx® against generic challengers in Hatch-Waxman litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of crystalline form patent validity, supporting patent protection strategies for blockbuster drugs and maintaining exclusivity periods against generic entry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry, as polymorph and salt form patents are confirmed as valid means of extending patent protection beyond base compound patents.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying a motion for attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Rule 11 sanctions where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 post-Alice.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the denial of sanctions and attorneys' fees, holding that the district court's order lacked sufficient detail to permit meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that continued to assert claims after the PTO rejected claims in related applications under § 101 following Alice and after a related patent was invalidated by another court. The decision signals heightened scrutiny of patent assertion where indicators of frivolousness are present.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers and fee applicants benefit from the requirement that district courts provide detailed reasoning when denying exceptional case findings, increasing accountability for questionable patent assertions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when pursuing infringement claims on patents with related applications rejected under § 101, particularly when prior art and invalidity indicators exist.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in oil and gas tool patent claims and whether the evidence supported findings of direct and induced infringement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment of infringement and remanded for further proceedings, addressing claim construction of the term 'internal diameter' in a patent directed to float tools used in oil and gas well casing operations. The case involves claims covering rupture disc assemblies used to reduce friction during casing insertion in wellbores, a commercially significant technology in the energy services sector.
impacts.positiveImplications: Energy service companies accused of infringement benefit from the vacatur, potentially narrowing the scope of asserted patent claims covering critical well completion tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas tools space face uncertainty about claim scope following remand, potentially weakening enforcement of patents covering widely-used downhole equipment.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to the outcome of an ex parte reexamination.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over a contract interpretation dispute regarding whether asserted patent claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, because the dispute was a state law contract matter that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit. This decision clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for disputes arising from patent settlement agreements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements gain clarity that contract interpretation disputes over settlement terms will be resolved in regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially providing more predictable outcomes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies with settlement agreements containing patent-contingent payment terms face the complexity of litigating in regional circuits that may have less expertise in patent-related contexts, and may face forum-shopping risks.

impacts.caseName: AML IP, LLC v. Bath & Body Works Direct, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may dismiss a patent infringement case on § 101 eligibility grounds after already determining that venue is improper.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal on both improper venue and patent ineligibility grounds. The court rejected AML's argument that after finding venue improper, the court should not have reached the § 101 merits. The '979 patent, directed to e-commerce methods using a 'bridge computer,' was held ineligible for patenting. This confirms that district courts retain authority to issue merits rulings even after finding venue deficient.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to obtain merits-based dismissals on eligibility grounds even when venue is also improper, providing preclusive effect that prevents patent holders from simply refiling in a proper venue.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and patent holders face the risk of receiving adverse § 101 rulings with potential preclusive effects even when their initial venue choice was incorrect, limiting their ability to pursue claims elsewhere.
